name: Central Lembata
catalog_citation: Fricke, Hanna. 2019. Traces of language contact: The Flores-Lembata languages in eastern Indonesia. PhD dissertation, Leiden University. LOT Dissertation Series 544. Utrecht: LOT.

catalog_quote: Stress in Central Lembata is marked by increased vowel length and higher pitch. In unstressed syllables, vowels can be reduced to schwa. In Central Lembata, the penultimate syllable of the word is stressed, unless the penultimate contains the vowel schwa. This becomes clear in suffixed nouns, such as kopong /ˈko.poŋ/ 'child' → kopong-u /ko.ˈpo.ŋu/ 'child-spec', which are both stressed on the penultimate syllable. ... However, in trisyllabic stems with final sequences of two identical vowels, the surface realisation shows ultimate stress, as in /tu.ˈlu.u/ 'repair' which is realised as [tuˈluː]. ... Schwa is the only penultimate vowel that cannot be stressed. Words with penultimate schwa are stressed at the ultimate syllable, such as /bə.ˈka/ 'to fly'. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every quoted string in the record is verbatim in the LOT 544 PDF we hold at book pp. 49-50 = PDF pp. 73-74, sec. 3.2.5-3.2.6, exactly as the locator says. (2) Deciding source: Fricke 2019 is a Leiden dissertation whose Part I is a full fieldwork grammar of Central Lembata; it is the only description of this language's phonology in existence (Glottolog has one descriptive ref, also by Fricke, on nouns/pronouns; Crossref shows no other author working on the language). The classification 'weight-hedged' (default penult, schwa penult -> ultima, hedged tendency to stress final CVC with free variation in C-final words, right edge) reproduces the source's own wording, including its hedge ('appears to be a tendency', 'apparent free variation'); sec. 3.8 restates the same rule.
